name: Data engineer
summary: Data engineer interviews usually focus on SQL, data modelling and building reliable pipelines that move and transform data at scale. Candidates commonly report hands-on SQL and Python or Scala questions, a discussion of tools such as Spark, Airflow, Kafka and cloud warehouses, and for experienced roles, a design round on building a pipeline or warehouse end to end.
rounds: SQL and coding screen: often advanced SQL plus Python
Data modelling and pipeline design: schemas, batch and streaming
Tools discussion: Spark, orchestration, warehouses and the cloud platform you've used
Project deep dive with the hiring manager
looks_for: Strong SQL, including window functions and query performance
Data modelling: facts, dimensions, and when to denormalise
Pipelines that can be rerun safely, are monitored, and recover cleanly
Data quality checks and clear ownership of data
How distributed processing and partitioning work
Awareness of what cloud data work costs

questions.text: Tell me about a pipeline that failed in production. How did you find and fix the problem?
covers: How it failed, and who noticed first
How you traced the cause: logs, data checks, changes upstream
The fix, the backfill, and the monitoring you added

questions.text: Describe a time people using your data found a problem in it before you did.
covers: What was wrong and how it affected them
How you corrected the data and kept them informed
The check you added so you'd catch it first next time

questions.text: Tell me about a time you made a pipeline much faster or cheaper to run.
covers: The starting runtime or cost
What you changed: partitioning, file formats, incremental loads, rewriting queries
The result in numbers

questions.text: Tell me about a time different teams defined the same metric differently. How did you sort it out?
covers: The metric and each team's version of it
How you reached one definition and documented it
How the change was rolled out to reports and users

questions.text: Explain the difference between ETL and ELT, and why many teams now load data first and transform it later.
covers: Transforming before loading versus transforming inside the warehouse
How scalable cloud warehouses changed the trade-off
When ETL still makes sense: sensitive data, heavy cleaning before storage

questions.text: How would you design a star schema for an online shop's sales reporting?
covers: A sales fact table at a clear grain, such as one row per order line
Dimensions for product, customer, date and channel
What happens when a dimension changes, such as a customer moving city

questions.text: What are slowly changing dimensions? Explain type 1 and type 2.
covers: Type 1 overwrites the old value; type 2 keeps history by adding new rows
Effective dates and a current-row flag
When the business actually needs the history

questions.text: What does it mean for a pipeline to be idempotent, and how do you make a daily job safe to rerun?
covers: The same result no matter how many times it runs
Overwriting partitions or merging on keys instead of blindly appending
Handling late-arriving data and backfills

questions.text: Batch or streaming: how would you decide for a new data feed?
covers: How fresh the data needs to be, and what it's used for
The extra cost and complexity of streaming tools such as Kafka and stream processors
Late, out-of-order and duplicate events

questions.text: A Spark job that used to take ten minutes now takes two hours. How would you investigate?
covers: Checking data volume and recent code or configuration changes
Using the Spark UI to look for skewed partitions, large shuffles and spills to disk
Fixes: repartitioning, broadcast joins, filtering early, sensible file sizes

questions.text: Explain partitioning, and why columnar file formats such as Parquet matter for analytics.
covers: Partitions let queries skip data they don't need
Columnar formats read only the needed columns and compress well
The problem of too many small files

questions.text: Talk me through building a pipeline that pulls data from a third-party API every hour.
covers: Scheduling with an orchestrator such as Airflow, with retries
Rate limits, pagination and pulling only what's new
Landing raw data first, then validating and transforming, with alerts on failure

questions.text: What data quality checks would you put on an important table?
covers: Row counts, nulls, uniqueness, valid ranges and freshness
Comparing totals between source and target
What happens when a check fails: stop the pipeline, alert, or set the bad rows aside

questions.text: Talk me through a SQL approach to remove duplicate records and keep only the latest one for each customer.
covers: ROW_NUMBER partitioned by customer and ordered by update time, newest first
Keeping only row number one
How ties and missing timestamps are handled

questions.text: How would you handle personal data such as email addresses and phone numbers on a data platform?
covers: Role-based access, and masking or hashing sensitive columns
Keeping only what's needed, and only for as long as needed
Supporting deletion requests and logging who accessed what

questions.text: Why data engineering rather than analytics or data science?
covers: Enjoying building the foundations other people rely on
An example project that shows it
What you want to learn next: streaming, cloud platforms, modelling

questions.text: What would you want to understand about our data platform in your first month?
covers: The main sources, pipelines and who uses the data
Known pain points: cost, reliability, data quality
How data work is prioritised between teams

tips: Practise SQL until window functions, CTEs and joins feel routine; most loops test them early.
Be able to draw one of your pipelines from source to dashboard, with its data volumes, schedule and failure handling.
Mention reruns, backfills and monitoring in any design answer; they separate working pipelines from demos.
Know why you chose each tool on your resume, and one weakness of each.
Talk about cost: cloud data work is often judged on what it costs to run as well as how fast it is.
